For people who have lived in New York, maybe native New Yorkers, Americans, who traveled to Taipei, um, are there any of these people online who spoke about their experiences on the similarities and differences between these two cities?




2/2

Worked for 1m 2s








Yes — there are quite a few, and I found several that are unusually close to what you're asking for: people who lived in NYC, sometimes for most of their adult lives, and then lived in or visited Taipei. What's interesting is that several of them independently make comparisons very similar to what you were noticing.
Probably the best match: “The Girl Who Ate Everything” — an American who had lived most of her adult life in NYC, then lived in Taipei. She wrote an entire long post specifically about adapting to Taipei from a New Yorker's perspective. She says adapting was surprisingly easy because of the reliable English-friendly MRT, abundant cheap food, low street crime, and 24-hour convenience stores. She also compares cycling in Taipei with Manhattan/Brooklyn and goes into dozens of mundane differences—garbage collection, restaurant customs, tipping, toilets, payment, rain, transportation, etc. 

Roboppy
An NYC public-school teacher who spent a month in Taipei actually said almost exactly what you're getting at. He wrote that his month there convinced him that “Taipei is close enough to NYC” that he could genuinely build a life there, specifically citing transit, convenience, crazy traffic, and proximity to outdoor sports. He was living in Brooklyn and working in NYC at the time. 

Reddit
 This is probably the most direct “these cities weirdly resemble each other” account I found.
Jeremy Wang, explicitly writing “as a New Yorker,” compared the Taipei MRT to the NYC MTA station-by-station. His immediate reaction was how dramatically cleaner Taipei was. But he also noticed structural similarities: ads everywhere, automated station announcements, lines becoming elevated farther from the center, and Taipei Main Station functioning somewhat like Grand Central. He even compares an above-ground Taipei segment with taking the F train toward Coney Island.

Jeremy Wang in Taiwan
Another NYC resident visited Taipei with his kids and wrote an entire “Taipei MRT appreciation post.” He compared working elevators, stroller-friendly gates, precise countdown clocks, bathrooms, platform doors, train frequency and airport connections with NYC. His conclusion was essentially that he dreaded returning to the MTA after experiencing Taipei. 

Reddit
 A different family from NYC said they understood Taipei's transportation system within a day. 

Reddit
Catherine, a Taiwanese-American who worked in NYC before moving to Da'an, gives one of the fullest lifestyle comparisons. She says Taipei's transit made her quality of life much better than her NYC experience; her NYC commute had been about two hours round-trip, while Taipei made spontaneous exploration easy. She found Taipei vastly cheaper, especially housing and eating out, and felt considerably safer as a woman: she described frequent verbal sexual harassment in NYC versus only a couple of incidents in Taipei. At the same time, she found Taipei street traffic “insane” and had to adjust to different conversational boundaries and less-direct workplace communication.

Expat Arrivals
There's even someone who has been splitting each year between Taipei, NYC, and Singapore. Their reaction is basically that Taipei “just fits.” They miss NYC's culinary scene, but prefer the extraordinary proximity Taipei offers to mountains, beaches, lakes and hot springs. 

Reddit
 That particular difference comes up repeatedly: Taipei provides big-city life without separating you nearly as much from nature.
And there's one especially interesting older New Yorker perspective: Yvette, who grew up in New York and later spent extended time with her family in Taiwan, said one of Taiwan's major attractions was precisely the mix of urban living and nature, which made life feel more balanced. Her family also found Taipei safe and easy to navigate. 

Gold Card Program
So after reading these, I think there's a pretty clear recurring theme:

Taipei often feels familiar to New Yorkers at the “urban operating system” level: dense neighborhoods, people everywhere, excellent transit, walking, apartments, convenience everywhere, late-night food, tiny businesses, chaotic traffic, and the ability to live without structuring your life around a car. One recent commenter even said that, for an American, NYC is the closest American analogue to Taipei in pace and density, although Taipei still feels denser to them.
